etymologies.etymologyHTML:
Inherited from Middle English foul, from Old English fūl (“foul, dirty, unclean, impure, vile, corrupt, rotten, stinking, guilty”), from Proto-West Germanic *fūl, from Proto-Germanic *fūlaz (“foul, rotten”), from Proto-Indo-European *puH- (“to rot”).

Cognate with Dutch vuil (“foul, dirty, filthy, obscene, lewd”), German faul (“foul, rotten, putrid, lazy”), German Low German fuul (“foul, rotten, putrid”), Faroese fúlur (“foul”), Icelandic fúll (“foul, rotten, sullen”), Danish ful (“nasty, ugly”), Norwegian Bokmål ful (“clever, sly”), Norwegian Bokmål ful (“clever, sly”) and Swedish ful (“ugly, dirty, bad”), and through Indo-European, with Albanian fëlliq (“to make dirty”), Latin puter (“rotten”). More at putrid.

Ancient Greek φαῦλος (phaûlos, “bad”) is a false cognate inasmuch as it is not from the same etymon, instead being cognate to few.

definitions.definition: Covered with, or containing unclean matter; dirty.

quote.citation: 1944 November and December, A Former Pupil, “Some Memories of Crewe Works—II”, in Railway Magazine, page 342:
quote.text: It was, however, most interesting work, and the moulders themselves were a decent crowd, never tired of making jokes about themselves such as the hoary one that moulders did not live long, which however ran counter to the other one that no germs could live in a foundry—the atmosphere was too foul.

quote.citation: 2013 June 29, “Unspontaneous combustion”, in The Economist, volume 407, number 8842, page 29:
quote.text: Since the mid-1980s, when Indonesia first began to clear its bountiful forests on an industrial scale in favour of lucrative palm-oil plantations, “haze” has become an almost annual occurrence in South-East Asia. The cheapest way to clear logged woodland is to burn it, producing an acrid cloud of foul white smoke that, carried by the wind, can cover hundreds, or even thousands, of square miles.

definitions.definition: (of words or a way of speaking) Obscene, vulgar or abusive.
Detestable, unpleasant, loathsome.

quote.citation: 1610–1611 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tempest”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act II, scene ii]:
quote.text: […] Hast thou forgot / The foul witch Sycorax, who with age and envy / Was grown into a hoop? Hast thou forgot her?

quote.citation: 1667, John Milton, “Book I”, in Paradise Lost. […], London:  […]  [Samuel Simmons], and are to be sold by Peter Parker […]; [a]nd by Robert Boulter […]; [a]nd Matthias Walker, […], →OCLC; republished as Paradise Lost in Ten Books: […], London: Basil Montagu Pickering […], 1873, →OCLC:
quote.text: Who first seduced them to that foul revolt?

quote.citation: 1982 March 18, Eric J. Cassel[l], “The Nature of Suffering and the Goals of Medicine”, in The New England Journal of Medicine, volume 306, number 11, →DOI, page 642:
quote.text: Cultural norms and social rules regulate whether someone can be among others or will be isolated, whether the sick will be considered foul or acceptable, and whether they are to be pitied or censured.

definitions.definition: Disgusting, repulsive; causing disgust.
(obsolete) Ugly; homely; poor.

quote.citation: c. 1602, William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Troylus and Cressida”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene iii]:
quote.text: Let us, like merchants, show our foulest wares.

definitions.definition: Unpleasant, stormy or rainy. (of the weather)

quote.citation: c. 1596 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Life and Death of King Iohn”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act IV, scene ii]:
quote.text: So foul a sky clears not without a storm.

definitions.definition: Dishonest or not conforming to the established rules and customs of a game, conflict, test, etc.
(nautical) Entangled and therefore restricting free movement, not clear.
(technical) (with "of") Positioned on, in, or near enough to (a specified area) so as to obstruct it.

quote.citation: 2015, Transportation Safety Board of Canada, Railway Investigation Report R13T0192[1]:
quote.text: The bus had stopped just foul of the north track at the Erindale Station Road public railway crossing […]  With the bus stationary, but still foul of the north track, the train struck one of its front mirrors.

definitions.definition: (baseball) Outside of the base lines; in foul territory.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: Inherited from Middle English foulen, fulen, from Old English fūlian (“to become foul; rot; decay”), from Proto-West Germanic *fūlēn, from Proto-Germanic *fūlāną (“to rot; decay”).

definitions.definition: (transitive) To make dirty.
(transitive) To besmirch.
(transitive) To clog or obstruct.

quote.citation: 1961 November, “Talking of Trains: Aircraft on rail tracks”, in Trains Illustrated, page 650:
quote.text: As a result of the accident at Southend Airport when a Hermes aircraft overshot the runway and fouled the down Shenfield to Southend Victoria line between Rochford and Prittlewell, the Eastern Region is considering warning arrangements, which have already been provided on some lines running past aerodromes.

definitions.definition: (transitive, nautical) To entangle.

quote.citation: 1941, Emily Carr, chapter 18, in Klee Wyck‎[2]:
quote.text: The Indian's heart was sore for his boat; it looked as if nothing could save her. She was drifting more slowly now, her propeller fouled in kelp.

definitions.definition: (transitive, basketball, soccer) To make contact with an opposing player in order to gain advantage.

quote.citation: 2011 January 8, Chris Bevan, “Arsenal 1 - 1 Leeds”, in BBC‎[3]:
quote.text: The Gunners dominated for long periods but, against the run of play, Denilson fouled Max Gradel and Robert Snodgrass put Leeds ahead from the spot.

definitions.definition: (intransitive, basketball, soccer) To commit a foul.

quote.citation: 2009, Brandon Lang, Stanley Cohen, Beating the Odds: The Rise, Fall, and Resurrection of a Sports Handicapper, →ISBN:
quote.text: State begins fouling and UCLA misses a couple of front-end free throws on one-and-ones.

definitions.definition: (transitive, baseball) To hit outside of the baselines.
(intransitive, baseball) To hit a ball outside of the baselines.
(intransitive) To become clogged.
(intransitive) To become entangled.
To come into contact or collide with.

quote.citation: 1963 July, “News and Comment: The future of coal by rail”, in Modern Railways, page 5:
quote.text: The full capacity, however, requires a hopper of a size that takes the wagon body up to 11ft 11½in above rail level, which would foul many existing colliery screens.

definitions.definition: (sports) A breach of the rules of a game, especially one involving inappropriate contact with an opposing player in order to gain an advantage; for example, tripping someone up in soccer, or contact of any kind in basketball.

quote.citation: 2011 December 10, Arindam Rej, “Norwich 4 - 2 Newcastle”, in BBC Sport‎[4]:
quote.text: A second Norwich goal in four minutes arrived after some dire Newcastle defending. Gosling gave the ball away with a sloppy back-pass, allowing Crofts to curl in a cross that the unmarked Morison powered in with a firm, 12-yard header.Gosling's plight worsened when he was soon shown a red card for a foul on Martin.

quote.citation: 2011, Charley Rosen, Crazy Basketball: A Life In and Out of Bounds, Lincoln, NE: University of Nebraska Press, →ISBN, page 216:
quote.text: Even though we were swept, we did outstat the Fast Breakers in one category: they had six technical fouls for the series (three for Bibby, two for Matthews, and one for Shouse), and we totaled nine (three each for Mannion and me, one each for Jose Slaughter, Lewis, and Lamp).

definitions.definition: (bowling) A (usually accidental) contact between a bowler and the lane before the bowler has released the ball.
(baseball) A foul ball, a ball which has been hit outside of the base lines.
